source.title: Conditioning of random Fourier feature matrices: double descent and generalization error

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Figure 2.1 is referenced and described, but its plotted values are not included in the text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests double descent in random-feature regression, a model setting distinct from the deep networks named in V1, using empirical risk curves and theoretical analysis.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own risk curves and explicitly states that risk exhibits double descent. It also reports condition-number curves, but those are not rows for the versions here, which concern risk. The plotted risk values are unavailable in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own empirical test-risk curves for random-feature regression as the feature count N varies against fixed m=100. It states that risk peaks at N/m=1 and reaches its global minimum in the overparameterized regime, so it bears on V4 in a non-deep-network model class. It also proves conditioning-based risk bounds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that risk in random-feature regression shows double descent as a consequence of condition-number double descent. Their bounds cover least-squares, min-norm interpolation and sparse regression. They add that the feature matrix needs no regularization to be well-conditioned, and that N/m need only be logarithmically far from the threshold for small risk.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes random-feature regression, with randomized features and a trained final layer, rather than measuring fully trained deep networks. Its empirical sweep varies feature count against a fixed sample count.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports risk curves for Fourier features with zero noise and with 10% SNR, and for ReLU features; it states that the double-descent behavior occurs in each reported experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: The condition number of the random feature matrix shows double descent, peaking at N/m=1 together with the risk. The paper proves ill-conditioning at N=m and good conditioning when N/m is logarithmically far from 1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The test-risk peak in random-feature regression coincides with, and is bounded through, a peak in the condition number of the feature matrix at the interpolation threshold.

record.peer_reviewed: Information and Inference A Journal of the IMA
record.problems: Empirical risk values are only shown in the referenced figure and are absent from the supplied text. The empirical curves average 10 random trials, but no uncertainty measure is stated. The reported setup fixes m and varies N, so it does not test epoch-wise behavior or whether increasing sample size raises risk.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant risk rows left out. Condition-number results were not included because they do not measure the risk behavior named in the claim versions.

untested.parts: No deep networks; only random-feature models with an untrained hidden layer.
No epoch-wise or training-time sweep; training uses a closed-form pseudo-inverse.
No sweep of sample size m at fixed N. Theoretical bounds are upper bounds and cannot show risk rising with more data.
Condition number is linked to the peak only along the N/m axis; there is no single effective-complexity measure across size, epochs and samples.
Peak size versus noise level is not compared, because curves are rescaled. No multiple descent and no tuned regularization; regularization is left to future work.

missing.what: Theoretical risk bounds (Theorems 4.1, 4.2, 4.4): risk is controlled by the condition number in the least-squares, min-norm and sparse regimes. Small risk needs N/m only logarithmically far from 1, without regularization, even with bounded noise.
Condition-number double-descent curves coinciding with the risk peak, and Theorem 3.1(c) proving ill-conditioning at N=m.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'challenges' label was removed. A peak without label noise does not contradict V6, which names variance as an alternative driver. The rescaled figure cannot show how noise affects the peak, and regularization is not tested. Mei & Montanari and Belkin et al. already show random-feature double descent; this study adds a conditioning-based proof. The empirical setup is small (d=3, m=100, 10 trials, no uncertainty reported).

versions.untested_parts: The study examines random-feature models, not deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or other training time is reported.
No test-risk sweep that increases sample size near the interpolation threshold is reported.
The reported model-class evidence is for random-feature regression; it does not establish the curve across all model classes.
The study links risk to matrix conditioning, but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and samples.
The experiments include zero-noise and noisy cases, but do not test multiple or triple descent, whether variance drives the peak, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes it.
No re-counting of complexity using an effective number of parameters is reported.
